title: Electricity
blurb: From Ohm's law to the fuse board in your hallway.

lessons.title: Voltage, current & resistance
lessons.summary: The three quantities behind every circuit, and the one law that ties them together.

cards.title: Electricity is moving charge
cards.text:
A current is a flow of electric charge. In a metal wire it's electrons nudging each other along. Each electron drifts slowly, but the push travels through the wire almost instantly, like water already filling a hose.

By convention, current is drawn flowing from + to −, the opposite way to the electrons. Every circuit diagram uses this convention.

cards.title: The water analogy
cards.text:
Picture a tank feeding a pipe.
• Voltage is the pressure, set by how high the water stands.
• Current is how much water flows per second.
• Resistance is a narrow section of pipe that limits the flow.

More pressure pushes more flow; a narrower pipe allows less. That's the whole idea behind Ohm's law.
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><rect class="w" x="42" y="55" width="66" height="83" rx="0"/><path class="s" d="M40 25 V140 H110 V25"/><path class="a" d="M42 55L108 55"/><rect class="w" x="110" y="119" width="70" height="12" rx="0"/><rect class="w" x="180" y="124" width="55" height="2" rx="0"/><rect class="w" x="235" y="119" width="65" height="12" rx="0"/><path class="s" d="M110 118 H180 V123 H235 V118 H300"/><path class="s" d="M110 132 H180 V127 H235 V132 H300"/><path class="r" d="M24 135L24 60"/><path class="r" d="M27.5 67.2L24 60L20.5 67.2"/><path class="r" d="M24 60L24 135"/><path class="r" d="M20.5 127.8L24 135L27.5 127.8"/><path class="a" d="M250 108L295 108"/><path class="a" d="M287.8 111.5L295 108L287.8 104.5"/><path class="a" d="M130 108L170 108"/><path class="a" d="M162.8 111.5L170 108L162.8 104.5"/></g><text class="r" x="78" y="168" text-anchor="middle">height ≈ voltage</text><text class="a" x="220" y="98" text-anchor="middle">flow ≈ current</text><text class="" x="208" y="152" text-anchor="middle">narrow ≈ resistance</text></svg>

cards.title: Ohm's law
cards.text: Voltage (volts, V) equals current (amps, A) times resistance (ohms, Ω). Cover the quantity you want in the triangle and the other two tell you how to get it.
example: 12 V battery across a 4 Ω heater
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><path class="s" d="M110 20 L20 160 H200 Z"/><path class="s" d="M62 95L158 95"/><path class="s" d="M110 95L110 160"/></g><text class="" x="110" y="82" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:34px">V</text><text class="" x="70" y="146" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:34px">I</text><text class="" x="150" y="146" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:34px">R</text><text class="a" x="268" y="62" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:22px">V = I × R</text><text class="a" x="268" y="98" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:22px">I = V ÷ R</text><text class="a" x="268" y="134" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:22px">R = V ÷ I</text></svg>

cards.title: Try it: dim the bulb
cards.text: Change the voltage and the resistance. Watch the current and the power the bulb turns into light and heat.

cards.title: It's the current that hurts
cards.text:
Your body is a resistor too. What matters for safety is how much current passes through it, and which way.
Around 1 mA you feel a tingle. Near 10 mA muscles can lock and you may not be able to let go. From roughly 50–100 mA across the chest, the heart can go into fibrillation.

That's why home RCDs trip at 30 mA: well before the dangerous zone.
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><rect class="rz" x="215" y="98" width="85" height="24" rx="2"/><path class="s" d="M20 110L300 110"/><path class="s" d="M40 103L40 117"/><path class="s" d="M120 103L120 117"/><path class="s" d="M170 103L170 117"/><path class="s" d="M250 103L250 117"/><path class="a" d="M170 72L170 102"/></g><text class="" x="40" y="92" text-anchor="middle">feel it</text><text class="" x="115" y="92" text-anchor="middle">can't let go</text><text class="a" x="170" y="64" text-anchor="middle">RCD trips</text><text class="r" x="255" y="92" text-anchor="middle">heart risk</text><text class="" x="40" y="140" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:16px">1 mA</text><text class="" x="120" y="140" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:16px">10 mA</text><text class="a" x="170" y="140" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:16px">30 mA</text><text class="r" x="250" y="140" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:16px">100 mA</text><text class="" x="160" y="172" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px">current through the body (log scale)</text></svg>

cards.title: Conductors and insulators
cards.text:
In metals, some electrons are free to move, so current flows easily: copper, aluminium, silver. In insulators such as plastic, rubber, glass and dry wood, electrons are held tightly and almost no current flows.

Cables combine both: a copper core inside a plastic jacket.

cards.title: Resistance of a wire
cards.text: A wire's resistance grows with its length and shrinks with its cross-section. That's why long cable runs need thicker cables, and why thin extension leads get warm.

cards.title: Measuring with units
cards.text: Prefixes keep the numbers manageable. A phone charger supplies about 2 A, a sensor draws a few milliamps, and the national grid carries kilovolts.

cards.title: Short circuits
cards.text: A short circuit is a path with almost no resistance between live and neutral. By Ohm's law, the current becomes enormous, heating cables in a fraction of a second. Fuses and breakers exist to cut it off before a fire starts.

cards.title: Open and closed circuits
cards.text: Current only flows around a complete loop. A switch simply opens the loop (off) or closes it (on). A broken wire, a blown fuse or a loose terminal all open the circuit.

quiz.q: A 9 V battery drives current through a 450 Ω resistor. What is the current?
quiz.explain: I = V ÷ R = 9 ÷ 450 = 0.02 A, which is 20 mA.

quiz.q: In the water analogy, what plays the role of voltage?
quiz.explain: Voltage is the push, like pressure. Flow is current; pipe narrowness is resistance.

quiz.q: You double the resistance and keep the voltage the same. The current…
quiz.explain: I = V ÷ R. Twice the R with the same V gives half the current.

quiz.q: Why do long cable runs need thicker cables?
options: Resistance grows with length, so a bigger cross-section compensates
quiz.explain: R = ρ × L ÷ A: more area offsets more length.

quiz.q: What does a switch do?
quiz.explain: Off = open loop, on = closed loop.

lessons.title: Circuits at home
lessons.summary: Series vs parallel, power, and what the breakers in your board actually do.

cards.title: Series vs. parallel
cards.text:
In series, components share a single loop. The same current flows through each and the voltage is split between them. One break stops everything, like old Christmas lights.

In parallel, each component has its own path to the supply. Each gets the full voltage and can be switched on or off independently.

cards.title: Your house is wired in parallel
cards.text:
Every socket and light hangs between the live (L) and neutral (N) conductors. That's why each appliance gets the full 230 V, and why switching off the kettle doesn't turn off the fridge.

The more you plug in, the more total current flows in the live wire. That total is what breakers watch.

cards.title: Power
cards.text: Power (watts) is how fast energy is used. Multiply the voltage by the current. Rearranged, I = P ÷ V tells you how much current an appliance draws.
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><path class="s bgf" d="M110 150 L120 70 H190 L200 150 Z"/><path class="s" d="M130 62L180 62"/><path class="s" d="M190 82 C232 82 232 140 197 140"/><path class="s" d="M120 92 L96 76 L101 70"/><rect class="s" x="100" y="150" width="110" height="9" rx="3"/><path class="a" d="M145 52 c-6 -8 6 -14 0 -22"/><path class="a" d="M165 52 c-6 -8 6 -14 0 -22"/></g><text class="r" x="275" y="82" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:22px">2300 W</text><text class="" x="275" y="110" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:20px">÷ 230 V</text><text class="a" x="275" y="140" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:24px">= 10 A</text></svg>

cards.title: Breakers vs. RCDs
cards.text:
A breaker (MCB) protects the cable. If too much current flows, the wire would overheat, so it trips. A 16 A breaker on a socket circuit is typical.

An RCD protects people. It compares the current going out on live with the current coming back on neutral. If about 30 mA is missing, it has leaked somewhere, maybe through a person, and it trips in a fraction of a second.
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><path class="r" d="M20 70L270 70"/><path class="s" d="M20 110L270 110"/><ellipse class="s" cx="150" cy="90" rx="16" ry="42"/><rect class="s bgf" x="270" y="58" width="36" height="64" rx="3"/><path class="r" d="M40 56L100 56"/><path class="r" d="M92.8 59.5L100 56L92.8 52.5"/><path class="a" d="M110 124L40 124"/><path class="a" d="M47.2 120.5L40 124L47.2 127.5"/></g><text class="r" x="70" y="46" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:16px">10.00 A out</text><text class="" x="75" y="142" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:16px">9.97 A back</text><text class="" x="288" y="95" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:15px">load</text><text class="r" x="200" y="170" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:18px">30 mA missing → trip!</text></svg>

cards.title: Reading your bill: kWh
cards.text: You pay for energy, not power. Energy = power × time, measured in kilowatt-hours (kWh). One kWh is 1 kW running for one hour.
cards.sketch: <svg viewBox="0 0 320 180" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2000/svg"><g class="d"><rect class="s" x="60" y="38" width="200" height="104" rx="8"/><rect class="s bgf" x="80" y="62" width="160" height="38" rx="3"/><circle class="a" cx="160" cy="122" r="6"/></g><text class="mono" x="160" y="89" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:20px">0 1 2 4 6.8</text><text class="a" x="230" y="128" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:18px">kWh</text><text class="" x="160" y="170" text-anchor="middle" style="font-size:17px">energy = power × time</text></svg>

cards.title: Typical home circuits
cards.text: In Portugal and much of Europe, homes are split into circuits, each with its own breaker: lighting, general sockets, kitchen, and big appliances like the oven or water heater.

cards.title: Standby power
cards.text: Many devices draw power even when "off": TV, router, chargers, coffee machine. Each may use only a few watts, but running all year, it adds up.

cards.title: Contracted power
cards.text: In Portugal you contract a maximum power with your supplier, such as 6.9 kVA. If you switch on too many appliances at once, the main breaker (ICP) trips. Higher contracted power means a higher fixed daily charge.

cards.title: Will it trip?
cards.text: Contracted power 6.9 kVA ≈ 30 A at 230 V. Oven (2 kW), kettle (2.2 kW) and washing machine heating (2 kW) together make 6.2 kW: close to the limit. Add a 2 kW heater and the main breaker trips.

cards.title: Plugs and sockets
cards.text: Portugal uses the Schuko-type socket (type F) with side earth clips. The UK uses type G with three rectangular pins and a fuse inside the plug.

quiz.q: Why does each socket in a house get the full 230 V?
options: Each socket has its own transformer
quiz.explain: In parallel, every load sits directly between live and neutral, so each sees the full supply voltage.

quiz.q: A 1150 W heater runs on 230 V. How much current does it draw?
What makes an RCD trip?
options: Current going out on live doesn't all return on neutral
quiz.explain: An RCD measures the imbalance between live and neutral. Overcurrent is the breaker's job.

quiz.q: A 1.5 kW oven runs for 4 hours. How much energy is that?
quiz.explain: 1.5 kW × 4 h = 6 kWh.

quiz.q: A 6.9 kVA contract allows roughly how much current at 230 V?
20 W of standby, all year, uses about…

lessons.title: AC and DC
lessons.summary: Why the socket alternates and the battery doesn't.

cards.title: Direct current
cards.text: In DC, current flows in one direction at a constant voltage. Batteries, solar panels and USB chargers supply DC, and every electronic circuit runs on it internally.

cards.title: Alternating current
cards.text: In AC, the voltage swings positive and negative in a smooth wave, reversing direction many times a second. European mains reverses 50 times a second: 50 hertz.

cards.title: Why 230 V isn't the peak
cards.text: Mains is quoted as 230 V, but that's the RMS value: the DC voltage that would deliver the same heating power. The actual peaks reach about 325 V.

cards.title: The war of the currents

events.l: Edison's DC station in New York
AC lights the Chicago World's Fair

cards.text: In the 1880s Edison promoted DC; Westinghouse and Tesla backed AC. AC won for power grids because transformers could easily step its voltage up for long-distance transmission and down for homes.

cards.title: Why AC for the grid?
cards.text: Power losses in cables depend on the square of the current. Transformers raise the voltage so the same power flows with far less current, and losses drop dramatically. Transformers only work with AC.

cards.title: Converters everywhere
cards.text: Your laptop charger turns AC into DC (a rectifier plus regulator). A solar inverter does the opposite, turning DC from panels into AC for the house.

cards.title: DC is coming back
cards.text: Modern electronics can convert DC voltages efficiently, so very long undersea and overland links now use high-voltage DC (HVDC). Data centres and EVs are also largely DC inside.

cards.title: Frequency is shared
cards.text: Every generator on a grid spins in sync. If demand suddenly exceeds supply, the frequency drops slightly below 50 Hz, and operators must add power within seconds to bring it back.

cards.title: The sine wave
cards.text: Generators produce a sine wave naturally because their coils rotate through a magnetic field. One full turn of a two-pole generator makes one cycle; at 3,000 rpm that's 50 cycles a second.

cards.title: Different countries, different mains
cards.text: Most of the world uses 220–240 V at 50 Hz. North America uses 120 V at 60 Hz, and Japan is split: 50 Hz in the east, 60 Hz in the west.

quiz.q: What does 50 Hz mean?
options: The current reverses direction 50 times a second (50 cycles)
quiz.explain: Hertz counts cycles per second.

quiz.q: Why did AC win for power grids?
options: Transformers can step its voltage up and down easily
quiz.explain: High voltage cuts transmission losses.

quiz.q: A solar inverter converts…
quiz.explain: Panels make DC; the house uses AC.

lessons.title: Magnetism and electromagnets
lessons.summary: How current makes magnetic fields and vice versa.

cards.title: Magnetic fields
cards.text: A magnet has a north and a south pole. Opposite poles attract; like poles repel. The invisible region where it acts is its magnetic field, which iron filings make visible as curved lines.

cards.title: Earth is a magnet

steps: Molten iron flows in the core

cards.text: Earth's molten iron core creates a magnetic field. A compass needle is a tiny magnet that lines up with it. Magnetic north drifts slowly and isn't exactly the geographic North Pole.

cards.title: Current makes a field
cards.text: In 1820 Ørsted noticed a compass needle twitch near a wire carrying current. Every current creates a magnetic field circling around it. This links electricity and magnetism.

cards.title: Electromagnets
cards.text: Wind wire into a coil and the fields add up. Put an iron core inside and the field becomes much stronger. Switch off the current and the magnet switches off too.

cards.title: Where electromagnets work
cards.text: Relays, door locks, loudspeakers, MRI scanners, scrapyard cranes and the contactors in your fuse board all use electromagnets.

cards.title: Relays
cards.text: A relay uses a small current through a coil to pull a switch closed. That lets a 3.3 V microcontroller safely switch a 230 V heater on and off.

cards.title: Induction
cards.text: Faraday discovered the reverse in 1831: a changing magnetic field pushes current through a nearby wire. Move a magnet in and out of a coil and current flows. This is how generators and transformers work.

cards.title: Induction hobs
cards.text: An induction hob runs high-frequency AC through a coil under the glass. The changing field induces currents directly in the iron pan, which heats up. The glass stays relatively cool, and non-magnetic pans don't work.

cards.title: Wireless charging
cards.text: Phone chargers use the same idea: a coil in the pad creates a changing field, and a coil in the phone picks it up. It's convenient but less efficient than a cable, and needs good alignment.

cards.title: Magnetic storage
cards.text: Hard drives store bits as tiny regions magnetised one way or the other. Credit-card stripes and old cassette tapes use the same principle.

quiz.q: What did Ørsted discover in 1820?
options: An electric current creates a magnetic field
quiz.explain: A compass needle moved near a current.

quiz.q: Why doesn't an aluminium pan work on an induction hob?
options: It isn't magnetic enough for the field to heat it efficiently
quiz.explain: Induction needs a ferromagnetic base.

quiz.q: A relay lets a small current…
quiz.explain: The coil pulls a separate contact closed.

lessons.title: Motors and generators
lessons.summary: Turning electricity into motion and back again.

cards.title: The motor effect
cards.text: A wire carrying current inside a magnetic field feels a force. Bend the wire into a loop on an axle and the forces on each side push in opposite directions: it turns.

cards.title: DC motors
cards.text: Small DC motors use a commutator, a split ring that reverses the current every half turn so the coil keeps spinning the same way. Brushes rub on it, which causes wear.

cards.title: Generators
cards.text: A generator is a motor in reverse: spin a coil in a magnetic field (or a magnet inside coils) and a voltage is induced. Turbines driven by steam, water or wind turn generators to make almost all our electricity.

cards.title: Induction motors
cards.text: Most industrial motors, pumps and fans are AC induction motors. The stator creates a rotating magnetic field; it induces currents in the rotor, which chases the field around. Simple, tough, no brushes.

cards.title: Motors use a lot of electricity

items.l: of world electricity runs motors (IEA estimate)

cards.text: Electric motors account for roughly 40–45% of global electricity use, according to the IEA, mostly in industry: pumps, compressors and fans. More efficient motors and speed control save huge amounts of energy.

cards.title: Variable speed drives
cards.text: A variable frequency drive (VFD) changes the frequency fed to an AC motor to control its speed. Since fan and pump power falls steeply with speed, running at 80% speed can use only about half the power.

cards.title: EV motors
cards.text: Electric cars use permanent-magnet or induction motors, often over 90% efficient, versus roughly 20–35% for petrol engines. They deliver full torque from standstill.

cards.title: Regenerative braking
cards.text: When an EV slows down, its motor runs as a generator, turning motion back into electricity to recharge the battery. That's why one-pedal driving extends range in city traffic.

cards.title: Stepper motors and servos
cards.text: Stepper motors move in exact steps (3D printers, CNC). Servos use feedback to hold a precise angle (robot arms, RC planes). Both are motion you can control precisely.

cards.title: Motor nameplates
cards.text: Every motor has a nameplate: rated power (kW), voltage, current, speed (rpm) and efficiency class (IE1 to IE5). It tells you what supply and protection it needs.

quiz.q: A generator is basically…
quiz.explain: Spinning it induces a voltage.

quiz.q: Why do variable speed drives save so much energy on fans?
options: Fan power falls with roughly the cube of speed
quiz.explain: A small speed cut gives a big power cut.

quiz.q: Regenerative braking…
options: Turns the motor into a generator to recharge the battery
quiz.explain: Kinetic energy becomes electricity.

lessons.title: The power grid
lessons.summary: From power station to your socket.

cards.title: Generation, transmission, distribution
cards.text: Electricity is generated in power stations and wind or solar farms, carried long distances on high-voltage transmission lines, then distributed at lower voltages to towns and homes.

cards.title: Transformers
cards.text: A transformer has two coils around an iron core. AC in the first coil creates a changing field that induces voltage in the second. The ratio of turns sets the ratio of voltages.

cards.title: Why high voltage?
cards.text: Cable losses equal I² × R. Doubling the voltage halves the current for the same power, cutting losses to a quarter.

cards.title: Balancing supply and demand
cards.text: Electricity is hard to store in bulk, so supply must match demand every second. Grid operators forecast demand and dispatch power plants, imports, storage and demand response to keep the balance.

cards.title: The daily demand curve
cards.text: Demand is low at night, rises in the morning and peaks in the evening when people cook and heat homes. Solar output peaks at midday, which is shifting when power is cheapest.

cards.title: Portugal's renewable mix
cards.text: Renewables (hydro, wind, solar and biomass) supply the majority of Portugal's electricity in a typical year, roughly 60–70% in recent years depending on rainfall and wind. In 2016, the country ran four days straight on renewables alone.

cards.title: Interconnections
cards.text: Portugal's grid is linked to Spain's, and Spain's to France. Interconnections let countries share surplus wind or solar, but the Iberian Peninsula's links to the rest of Europe are relatively limited.

cards.title: The April 2025 blackout
cards.text: On 28 April 2025, a sudden loss of generation triggered a cascade that blacked out almost all of mainland Spain and Portugal for many hours. Restoring a grid from zero ("black start") is slow and delicate.

cards.title: Storage on the grid
cards.text: Pumped hydro stores energy by pumping water uphill when power is cheap and releasing it through turbines when needed. Large batteries now respond in milliseconds to stabilise frequency.

cards.title: Smart grids
cards.text: Smart meters, sensors and automation let the grid see where power flows in real time, integrate rooftop solar and EVs, and reroute around faults automatically.

quiz.q: Why is electricity transmitted at very high voltage?
options: Less current is needed, so cable losses are much lower
quiz.explain: Losses scale with current squared.

quiz.q: A transformer works because…
options: A changing magnetic field induces a voltage in the second coil
quiz.explain: It relies on AC induction.

quiz.q: Pumped hydro storage…
options: Pumps water uphill when power is cheap and generates later
quiz.explain: It stores energy as height.

lessons.title: Batteries
lessons.summary: Chemistry, capacity and how to make them last.

cards.title: How a battery works
cards.text: A battery has two electrodes separated by an electrolyte. A chemical reaction pushes electrons out of one electrode, through your circuit, and back into the other. Recharging reverses the reaction.

cards.title: Capacity: Ah and Wh
cards.text: Amp-hours (Ah) say how much charge a battery holds. Multiply by voltage to get energy in watt-hours (Wh), which is what really matters for comparing batteries.

cards.title: Battery chemistries
cards.text: Lead-acid is cheap and heavy (car starter batteries). Lithium-ion packs far more energy per kilo (phones, laptops, EVs). LFP, a lithium iron phosphate variant, trades a little energy density for safety and long life.

cards.title: C-rate
cards.text: The C-rate compares charge or discharge current with capacity. 1C fully charges or empties a battery in about an hour; 0.5C in two hours; 3C in 20 minutes. High C-rates create heat and wear.

cards.title: State of charge and cycles
cards.text: Lithium batteries last longer if kept away from 0% and 100% for long periods. Many EVs recommend charging to 80% for daily use and 100% only before long trips.

cards.title: Why batteries age
cards.text: Each cycle causes tiny chemical changes that slowly reduce capacity. Heat speeds this up a lot. High charge levels and very fast charging add stress too.

cards.title: Cycle life
cards.text: LFP cells can often manage several thousand full cycles before falling to 80% capacity, which is why they're popular for home storage. Typical NMC cells manage fewer, but store more energy per kilo.

cards.title: Battery management systems
cards.text: A BMS watches every cell's voltage and temperature, balances them, limits current and disconnects the pack if anything goes wrong. Lithium packs must never be used without one.

cards.title: Thermal runaway
cards.text: If a lithium cell is damaged, overcharged or overheated, it can start a self-heating reaction that spreads to neighbouring cells. Such fires are hard to extinguish and can reignite.

cards.title: Series and parallel packs
cards.text: Cells in series add voltage; cells in parallel add capacity. An EV pack might combine about 100 groups in series to reach roughly 400 V.

quiz.q: A 12 V, 50 Ah battery stores about…
Charging at 0.5C takes roughly…
What speeds up battery ageing the most?
quiz.explain: Heat and high states of charge add stress.

lessons.title: Solar power
lessons.summary: How panels turn sunlight into electricity.

cards.title: The photovoltaic effect
cards.text: A solar cell is a thin slice of silicon with two differently treated layers. Light knocks electrons loose, and the junction between the layers pushes them in one direction: a DC current.

cards.title: Cells, panels, strings
cards.text: A cell makes about 0.5–0.6 V. Dozens of cells in series make a panel; several panels in series make a string with a few hundred volts, feeding an inverter.

cards.title: Watt-peak
cards.text: Panels are rated in watt-peak (Wp): output under standard test conditions of 1,000 W/m² of sunlight at 25 °C. Real output is usually lower because of heat, angle and dust.

cards.title: How much will it produce?
cards.text: In Portugal, each kWp of well-oriented panels typically produces around 1,400–1,700 kWh a year, among the best in Europe.

cards.title: Orientation and tilt
cards.text: In Portugal, panels facing south at around 30–35° give the most energy over a year. East–west layouts produce less in total but spread production across the day.

cards.title: Shade matters
cards.text: A small shadow on one cell can cut a whole string's output, because cells in series carry the same current. Bypass diodes and optimisers limit the damage.

cards.title: Heat lowers output
cards.text: Silicon cells lose roughly 0.3–0.4% of output per °C above 25 °C. On a hot summer roof the cells can reach 60 °C, losing over 10%.

cards.title: Self-consumption

items: Charge the EV in the sun
Add a battery for the evening

cards.text: Solar power is worth most when you use it as it's produced, because exported power earns less than imported power costs. Run the dishwasher, heat water or charge the car at midday.

cards.title: Inverters
cards.text: String inverters convert DC from the panels into AC for the home. Hybrid inverters can also charge and discharge a battery. Microinverters sit behind each panel.

cards.title: Payback
cards.text: In sunny Portugal, a home system often pays for itself in roughly 5–8 years, depending on price, self-consumption and tariffs. Panels typically carry 25-year performance warranties.

quiz.q: What does "Wp" stand for?
options: Watt-peak, output under standard test conditions
quiz.explain: Rated at 1,000 W/m² and 25 °C.

quiz.q: Which direction should panels face in Portugal for maximum yearly energy?
quiz.explain: The sun crosses the southern sky.

quiz.q: Why do hot panels produce less?
options: Silicon cells lose efficiency as temperature rises
quiz.explain: About 0.35% per °C above 25 °C.

lessons.title: Choosing cables
lessons.summary: Cross-sections, voltage drop and why size matters.

cards.title: Cables heat up
cards.text: Every cable has some resistance, so current heats it (I² × R). Too small a cable for the current overheats, damages its insulation and can start a fire.

cards.title: Cross-section in mm²
cards.text: Cable size is the copper area in square millimetres. Bigger area, lower resistance, more current it can safely carry.

cards.title: Typical sizes at home
cards.text: Common practice in Portugal: 1.5 mm² for lighting, 2.5 mm² for sockets, 4 mm² for ovens or water heaters, 6 mm² for an EV charger or big heat pump. Always check the installation rules and the installer's calculation.

cards.title: The breaker protects the cable

items.r: rewire with thicker cable if needed

cards.text: The breaker must be rated so the cable can never carry more than it safely can. Swapping a 16 A breaker for a 25 A one "because it keeps tripping" removes the protection.

cards.title: Voltage drop
cards.text: Long cables lose voltage along the way. Rules usually limit the drop to a few percent. Single-phase drop is roughly twice the length times current times resistance per metre.

cards.title: Installation method matters
cards.text: A cable buried in insulation or bundled with others can't shed heat, so it carries less current safely than one in open air.

cards.title: Colours
cards.text: In Europe: brown is live (phase), blue is neutral, green-and-yellow is protective earth. Older Portuguese installations may use different colours, so never trust colours alone.

cards.title: Flexible vs rigid
cards.text: Fixed wiring uses solid or stranded rigid conductors. Appliance leads and extension cords use flexible multi-strand cable that survives bending.

cards.title: Extension leads

items: Check the max watts on the label

cards.text: A reel extension must be fully unrolled for high loads, otherwise the coiled cable traps heat and can melt. Never daisy-chain multi-plug adapters for heaters or kettles.

cards.title: Aluminium vs copper
cards.text: Aluminium conducts about 60% as well as copper, so it needs a bigger cross-section, but it's lighter and cheaper. Overhead power lines use aluminium; home wiring uses copper.

quiz.q: Which wire colour is protective earth in Europe?
quiz.explain: Brown live, blue neutral, green-yellow earth.

quiz.q: A 2.5 mm² socket circuit keeps tripping its 16 A breaker. What's right?
options: Find the overload or split the circuit
quiz.explain: The breaker protects the cable.

quiz.q: Why must a reel extension be unrolled for big loads?
options: Coiled cable can't shed heat and may melt
quiz.explain: The coil traps the heat.

lessons.title: Earthing and protection
lessons.summary: Breakers, RCDs, earth and surge protection.

cards.title: What earthing does
cards.text: Metal cases of appliances are connected to earth. If a live wire touches the case, current rushes to earth instead of through you, and a protective device trips.

cards.title: The earth electrode
cards.text: In many homes the earth connection ends at a copper rod or ring buried in the ground. Its resistance must be low enough for protective devices to work, and it should be tested periodically.

cards.title: Miniature circuit breakers
cards.text: An MCB trips two ways: a bimetallic strip for slow overloads (heat), and an electromagnet for short circuits (instant). The letter (B, C, D) sets how sensitive it is to inrush currents.

cards.title: MCB curves

viz.unit: magnetic trip (× rated current, upper bound)

cards.text: Type B trips magnetically at 3–5× its rating, good for homes. Type C at 5–10×, for motors and lighting with big inrush. Type D at 10–20×, for heavy industrial motors.

cards.title: RCD types

items: Type A: AC and pulsing DC

cards.text: Type AC detects only AC leakage. Type A also detects pulsing DC from electronics. Type B detects smooth DC too, often required for EV chargers and some solar inverters (or Type A with a DC-detection device).

cards.title: RCBOs
cards.text: An RCBO combines an MCB and an RCD in one device, so a fault on one circuit only trips that circuit instead of the whole house.

cards.title: Surge protection
cards.text: Lightning and grid switching can cause voltage spikes of thousands of volts for microseconds. A surge protection device (SPD) in the fuse board diverts them to earth, protecting electronics.

cards.title: Test your RCD
cards.text: RCDs have a test button that simulates a leak. Pressing it every few months checks that the mechanism isn't stuck. If it doesn't trip, call an electrician.

cards.title: Double insulation
cards.text: Some appliances have no earth wire: they're double insulated, shown by a square inside a square. Two layers of insulation protect you instead of an earth connection.

cards.title: Fuses
cards.text: A fuse is a thin wire that melts when too much current flows. It works only once and must be replaced with the same rating. Old Portuguese installations may still have them; modern boards use breakers.

quiz.q: Which RCD detects smooth DC leakage, as needed for many EV chargers?
quiz.explain: Type B covers smooth DC.

quiz.q: Why use RCBOs on each circuit?
options: A fault only trips that circuit
quiz.explain: Faults stay local.

quiz.q: What does an SPD protect against?
options: Short voltage spikes from lightning or switching
quiz.explain: It diverts surges to earth.

lessons.title: Three-phase power
lessons.summary: Why industry, big heat pumps and fast chargers use three wires.

cards.title: Three waves, offset
cards.text: Three-phase supply has three live conductors, each carrying an AC wave shifted by a third of a cycle (120°). At any moment at least one phase is near its peak, so power flows smoothly.

cards.title: 230 V and 400 V
cards.text: Between any phase and neutral you get 230 V; between two phases you get 400 V. Homes with three-phase supply still use 230 V for normal sockets.

cards.title: Three-phase power
example: 16 A per phase at 400 V, cos φ = 1
cards.text: Three-phase carries about three times the power of a single phase with the same current per wire.

cards.title: Why industry loves it
cards.text: Three-phase motors are simpler, smaller and self-starting, and transmission needs less copper for the same power. Nearly all generation, transmission and industrial loads are three-phase.

cards.title: Three-phase at home
cards.text: Larger homes in Portugal may have three-phase supply. It allows more contracted power, 11 kW or 22 kW EV charging, and big heat pumps, while circuits are spread across phases.

cards.title: Balancing the phases
cards.text: Loads should be spread evenly across the three phases. If one phase carries most of the load, it may trip while the others are lightly used, and the neutral carries extra current.

cards.title: Phase rotation
cards.text: The order in which phases peak (L1, L2, L3) sets the direction a three-phase motor turns. Swap any two phases and the motor runs backwards: a classic commissioning check.

cards.title: Star and delta
cards.text: Three-phase windings can be connected in star (Y), with a shared neutral point, or delta (Δ), in a triangle. Large motors often start in star to limit current, then switch to delta.

cards.title: Grids are three-phase worldwide

steps: Houses spread across L1, L2, L3

cards.text: From the generator to the distribution transformer on your street, power travels as three-phase. Each house on a single-phase supply is connected to one of the three phases.

cards.title: Spotting it

items: Three voltage readings on the meter
Brown, black and grey phase wires

cards.text: A three-phase board has three-pole or four-pole breakers and often a red CEE socket (5-pin) for machines. Three-phase meters show three readings.

quiz.q: Voltage between two phases of a European three-phase supply is about…
How do you reverse a three-phase motor?
quiz.explain: Changing the phase order reverses the rotating field.

quiz.q: Roughly how much power does 16 A per phase at 400 V give?

lessons.title: Power factor
lessons.summary: Real power, reactive power and why the grid cares.

cards.title: Real and apparent power
cards.text: With some loads, current and voltage don't peak at the same time. Then volts × amps (apparent power, in VA) is larger than the useful power that actually does work (real power, in W).

cards.title: The beer analogy
cards.text: Picture a glass of beer: the liquid is real power that quenches thirst; the foam is reactive power that takes space but does no work. The whole glass is apparent power.

cards.title: What causes it
cards.text: Motors, transformers and fluorescent ballasts store energy in magnetic fields each cycle and give it back, so their current lags the voltage. Cheap electronics distort the current wave.

cards.title: Why it matters
cards.text: A low power factor means more current for the same useful work: bigger cables, more losses, larger transformers. Utilities charge industrial customers for reactive energy.

cards.title: Correction with capacitors
cards.text: Capacitors draw current that leads the voltage, cancelling a motor's lagging current. Factories install capacitor banks to bring the power factor close to 1.

cards.title: Units: W, VA, var
cards.text: Real power in watts (W), reactive power in volt-amperes reactive (var), apparent power in volt-amperes (VA). UPS units and generators are rated in VA because their wiring must handle the full current.

cards.title: The power triangle
cards.text: Real and reactive power are at right angles, so apparent power is the hypotenuse: VA² = W² + var². The angle between them is φ.

cards.title: Your home bill
cards.text: Households in Portugal pay for active energy (kWh) only; reactive energy charges apply to larger commercial and industrial customers. Your contracted power, though, is in kVA.

cards.title: Power factor of devices
cards.text: Resistive loads like kettles and heaters have a power factor of 1. Motors run around 0.8–0.9 at full load and much lower when lightly loaded.

cards.title: PFC in chargers
cards.text: Larger electronic power supplies, including laptop and EV chargers, contain power factor correction circuits that make the current follow the voltage wave, as required by EU rules.

quiz.q: A load draws 1,000 VA with a power factor of 0.8. Its real power is…
quiz.explain: W = VA × cos φ = 800 W.

quiz.q: What corrects a lagging power factor in a factory?
quiz.explain: Capacitors cancel the lagging current.

quiz.q: Which device has a power factor of about 1?
quiz.explain: Pure resistance keeps current in step with voltage.

lessons.title: Using a multimeter
lessons.summary: Measuring volts, amps, ohms and continuity safely.

cards.title: One tool, many meters
cards.text: A multimeter measures voltage, current and resistance, and usually continuity, diodes and sometimes capacitance and temperature. A rotary dial chooses the function and range.

cards.title: Measuring voltage
cards.text: Set the dial to V (AC ~ or DC ⎓), put the probes across the two points, in parallel. The meter has very high resistance, so it barely disturbs the circuit.

cards.title: Measuring current

items: red lead in A or mA

cards.text: Current must flow through the meter, in series: break the circuit and insert the meter. Move the red lead to the A or mA socket. Forgetting to move it back is the classic way to blow the meter's fuse.

cards.title: Resistance and continuity
cards.text: Measure resistance only on unpowered circuits. Continuity mode beeps when the resistance is very low: perfect for finding broken wires or checking which cable is which.

cards.title: CAT ratings

items: CAT IV: supply origin, meter tails
CAT III: fuse boards, fixed wiring

cards.text: Meters carry a category rating for where they're safe to use. CAT II covers plugged-in appliances, CAT III the fixed installation and fuse boards, CAT IV the supply origin. Use at least CAT III 600 V on house wiring.

cards.title: Clamp meters
cards.text: A clamp meter measures current without breaking the circuit: you clamp it around a single conductor and it reads the magnetic field. Clamp around the whole cable and live and neutral cancel out.

cards.title: Auto-range and True RMS
cards.text: Auto-ranging meters pick the range for you. True RMS meters measure non-sinusoidal waveforms (from inverters, LED drivers, VFDs) correctly; cheaper meters can be quite wrong on these.

cards.title: Checking a socket
cards.text: To check a socket is live, measure between live and neutral (about 230 V), live and earth (about 230 V) and neutral and earth (near 0 V). Proper socket testers also check earth and RCD.

cards.title: Prove dead before you touch

steps: Test tester on a live source

cards.text: Before working on any circuit: isolate it, lock it off, test it's dead with a proven tester, and re-check the tester on a known live source. Never trust a switch or a label alone.

cards.title: Reading batteries and sensors
cards.text: Multimeters are great for electronics: battery health (a "12 V" battery should read about 12.6 V when full), sensor outputs, and checking a 3.3 V rail on an ESP32 board.

quiz.q: To measure current, the meter must be…
options: In series, so current flows through it
quiz.explain: Current is measured in series.

quiz.q: Why are clamp meters useful?
options: They measure current without breaking the circuit
quiz.explain: They sense the magnetic field around a conductor.

quiz.q: What must you do before working on a circuit you switched off?
options: Prove it dead with a tester you've checked on a live source
quiz.explain: Prove dead, and prove the tester works.

lessons.title: Charging electric cars
lessons.summary: AC, DC, kW and why charging slows down.

cards.title: AC charging
cards.text: At home and on most street posts, the car receives AC and converts it to DC with its own on-board charger. The car's charger limits the speed, usually 7–11 kW.

cards.title: DC fast charging
cards.text: Fast chargers convert AC to DC in the station and feed the battery directly, bypassing the car's charger. Powers range from 50 kW to 350 kW.

cards.title: Charging power options
cards.text: A normal socket gives about 2.3 kW (10 A at 230 V), slow but fine overnight for short commutes. A single-phase wallbox at 32 A gives about 7.4 kW.

cards.title: How long will it take?
cards.text: Divide the energy needed by the charging power, then add some margin for losses and the slower final stage.

cards.title: The charging curve
cards.text: DC charging is fastest at low states of charge and slows down as the battery fills, to protect it. Going from 10% to 80% often takes about as long as 80% to 100%.

cards.title: 400 V and 800 V cars
cards.text: Most EVs use about 400 V packs. Some newer cars, such as the XPeng G9 and Porsche Taycan, use 800 V platforms, which allow higher charging power with less current and heat.

cards.title: Connectors in Europe
cards.text: Type 2 is the standard AC plug in Europe. CCS2 adds two big DC pins below it for fast charging. Older Japanese cars may use CHAdeMO.

cards.title: Smart charging at home
cards.text: Smart wallboxes can follow cheaper night tariffs, use surplus solar, and reduce power if the house is near its contracted limit (load balancing), so the main breaker doesn't trip.

cards.title: Mobi.E in Portugal

steps: Choose a supplier card or app
Plug in at any Mobi.E point

cards.text: Portugal's public charging network is coordinated by Mobi.E. You can use most public chargers with one card or app from any supplier (CEME), and pay the operator, the supplier and network fees.

cards.title: Efficiency and losses
cards.text: Some energy is lost as heat while charging, typically about 10% for AC home charging, sometimes more at very low power. The meter at the wallbox shows more kWh than the battery receives.

quiz.q: Who converts AC to DC during home AC charging?
quiz.explain: AC charging uses the car's own charger.

quiz.q: Why does fast charging slow above about 80%?
options: To protect the battery as it fills
quiz.explain: The battery management system tapers the current.

quiz.q: Adding 40 kWh with an 11 kW charger takes about…

lessons.title: Energy at home
lessons.summary: Bills, tariffs and where the kWh go.

cards.title: Reading the bill
cards.text: A Portuguese electricity bill has a fixed part (contracted power, per day), an energy part (per kWh), network access charges, taxes (VAT, the audiovisual contribution) and sometimes discounts.

cards.title: Time-of-use tariffs

items: worth it if you shift load

cards.text: Simple tariffs charge the same price all day. Two-period (bi-horário) tariffs have cheaper off-peak (vazio) hours, mostly at night and weekends; three-period (tri-horário) splits peak and shoulder hours too.

cards.title: When bi-horário pays off
cards.text: It usually pays if you can move a good share of your consumption, often around 40% or more, to off-peak hours: EV charging, water heating, washing machine and dishwasher on a timer.

cards.title: Where the kWh go
cards.text: In a typical home, heating and hot water are the biggest users, followed by cooking, refrigeration, laundry and lighting. An EV can easily double household consumption.

cards.title: The fridge runs all year
cards.text: A fridge-freezer cycles on and off 24/7. A modern efficient one uses about 150–250 kWh a year; an old one can use two or three times more.

cards.title: Energy labels
cards.text: EU energy labels rate appliances from A (best) to G and show annual consumption in kWh. The scale was rescaled in 2021, so a new "C" can be better than an old "A+++".

cards.title: LED lighting
cards.text: LED bulbs use about 80–90% less electricity than old incandescent bulbs for the same light and last much longer. Light output is measured in lumens, not watts.

cards.title: Water heaters
cards.text: An electric water heater (termoacumulador) is often one of the biggest single loads. A timer for cheap hours, a lower thermostat setting (around 50–55 °C), and good insulation cut costs. Heat pump water heaters use about a third of the energy.

cards.title: Monitoring

steps: Clamp sensor on the main cable

cards.text: Smart meters and clamp-based monitors (for example with Home Assistant) show consumption in real time, revealing standby loads and expensive habits.

cards.title: Self-consumption communities
cards.text: In Portugal, neighbours, businesses and municipalities can form renewable energy communities and share solar production through the grid, paying network fees on shared energy.

quiz.q: On a bi-horário tariff, when is energy cheaper?
options: Off-peak hours, mostly at night and weekends
quiz.explain: Vazio hours are the cheap period.

quiz.q: Roughly how much less electricity does an LED use than an incandescent bulb for the same light?
quiz.explain: About 8 W versus 60 W.

quiz.q: Which is usually one of the largest single loads at home?
quiz.explain: Heating water takes a lot of energy.

lessons.title: Heating and cooking with electricity
lessons.summary: Resistive heat, heat pumps, ovens and hobs.

cards.title: Resistive heating
cards.text: Heaters, kettles, ovens and water heaters turn electricity into heat through resistance: 1 kWh of electricity gives 1 kWh of heat. That's 100% efficient, yet still expensive compared with a heat pump.

cards.title: Heat pumps: 3 to 4 times better

viz.unit: kWh of heat per kWh of electricity

cards.text: A heat pump moves heat from outside air (or the ground) into the house. Typical seasonal efficiency (SCOP) is 3–4: 1 kWh of electricity delivers 3–4 kWh of heat.

cards.title: Air-to-air vs air-to-water
cards.text: Air-to-air heat pumps are the familiar split air conditioners that also heat. Air-to-water units heat water for radiators, underfloor heating and hot taps.

cards.title: Oil-filled vs convector vs radiant
cards.text: All resistive heaters give the same heat per kWh. They differ in how they deliver it: oil-filled radiators are slow and steady, convectors warm air quickly, radiant panels warm people and objects directly.

cards.title: Kettles: heat only what you need
cards.text: A 2 kW kettle boils 1 litre in about 3 minutes. Boiling a full kettle for one cup wastes energy and time.

cards.title: Induction vs ceramic vs gas
cards.text: Induction heats the pan directly and is about 85–90% efficient. Ceramic (radiant) hobs are around 70%, gas burners around 40–55%. Induction is also faster and easier to control.

cards.title: Ovens and air fryers
cards.text: Heating a large oven cavity takes energy before any cooking starts. Small appliances like air fryers and microwaves heat less volume and often use far less energy for small portions.

cards.title: Thermostats and timers
cards.text: Every degree lower on the thermostat saves roughly 5–10% of heating energy. Timers and smart thermostats heat rooms only when they're used.

cards.title: Insulation first
cards.text: The cheapest kWh is the one you don't need. Roof and wall insulation, better windows and draught sealing reduce heating needs before you upgrade the heater.

cards.title: Portugal's cold homes
cards.text: Despite the mild climate, many Portuguese homes are poorly insulated and cold in winter. Portugal has had one of the higher rates of energy poverty in the EU, which is why efficiency programmes subsidise insulation and heat pumps.

quiz.q: A heat pump with a SCOP of 4 using 1,000 kWh delivers about…
quiz.explain: Heat = SCOP × electricity.

quiz.q: Which hob puts the most energy into the pan?
quiz.explain: Induction heats the pan directly.

quiz.q: Do all resistive electric heaters give the same heat per kWh?
options: Yes, 1 kWh in gives 1 kWh of heat
quiz.explain: They differ in delivery, not efficiency.

lessons.title: Static electricity and lightning
lessons.summary: Sparks, storms and lightning protection.

cards.title: Static charge
cards.text: Rubbing two materials together transfers electrons from one to the other. One becomes negatively charged, the other positively. The charge stays put ("static") until it finds a path.

cards.title: Why you get shocks
cards.text: Walking on carpet in dry weather builds up charge on your body, sometimes thousands of volts. Touch a metal door handle and it discharges in a tiny spark. Harmless to you, but deadly for electronics.

cards.title: ESD and electronics
cards.text: Electrostatic discharge can destroy chips with voltages too small to feel. That's why boards ship in anti-static bags and technicians wear wrist straps.

cards.title: How lightning forms
cards.text: Inside storm clouds, ice crystals and soft hail collide in strong updrafts, separating charge. The top of the cloud becomes positive and the bottom negative, until the air breaks down in a giant spark.

cards.title: Lightning numbers
cards.text: A typical lightning bolt carries around 30,000 amps, at hundreds of millions of volts, for a few microseconds, and heats the air to around 30,000 °C, about five times hotter than the Sun's surface.

cards.title: Lightning rods
cards.text: A lightning rod offers an easy path to earth, so a strike flows safely down a conductor instead of through the building. Benjamin Franklin popularised them in the 1750s.

cards.title: Safe in a car

items.r: the metal body carries the current around you

cards.text: A metal car body acts as a Faraday cage: current flows around the outside of the metal shell, not through the people inside. It's the metal, not the rubber tyres, that protects you.

cards.title: Outdoor safety

items: Wait 30 minutes after the last thunder

cards.text: If thunder is audible, you're within striking distance. Go indoors or into a car, stay away from tall isolated trees, hilltops and water, and wait 30 minutes after the last thunder.

cards.title: Surges into homes
cards.text: A nearby strike can induce surges in power and telephone lines that damage electronics. Surge protection devices at the fuse board and on sensitive equipment help.

cards.title: Static in industry
cards.text: Flowing fuel, powders and plastic films can build up dangerous static. Fuel stations, grain silos and paint shops use earthing and bonding to prevent sparks that could ignite vapours or dust.

quiz.q: Why are you safe inside a car during lightning?
options: The metal body conducts the current around you
Cars are too low to be hit
quiz.explain: It acts as a Faraday cage.

quiz.q: Static shocks are more common when…
quiz.explain: Dry air lets charge build up.

quiz.q: A typical lightning current is around…
quiz.explain: Tens of thousands of amps for microseconds.

lessons.title: Electrical safety
lessons.summary: Rules that keep people and homes safe.

cards.title: Three dangers
cards.text: Electricity hurts in three ways: electric shock (current through the body), burns (from arcs or hot surfaces) and fire (from overheating cables or connections).

cards.title: Current path matters
cards.text: Current from hand to hand or hand to foot crosses the chest and heart, the most dangerous paths. Wet skin has much lower resistance, letting more current flow at the same voltage.

cards.title: Water and electricity

items: Never use mains devices in the bath

cards.text: Bathrooms and kitchens have special rules: zones around baths and showers limit which equipment can go where, and all circuits should be protected by a 30 mA RCD.

cards.title: Loose connections
cards.text: A loose screw terminal has a small contact area and higher resistance, so it heats up, oxidises and heats further. Many electrical fires start at a connection, not in the middle of a cable.

cards.title: Warning signs
cards.text: Call an electrician if you see scorch marks, smell burning plastic, hear crackling, feel warm sockets or switches, or if breakers trip repeatedly.

cards.title: If someone is being shocked
cards.text: Don't touch them while they're in contact with the source. Switch off the power or separate them with something dry and non-conductive, call 112, and start CPR if needed.

cards.title: DIY limits
cards.text: Changing a light bulb or plugging in appliances is fine. New circuits, fuse-board work and anything in the fixed installation should be done by a qualified electrician, and in Portugal new installations need certification.

cards.title: Overloaded adapters

items.r: one high-power appliance per wall socket

cards.text: Plugging several high-power appliances into one multi-way adapter can overload it and the socket behind it. Heaters, kettles and irons should each have their own wall socket.

cards.title: Overhead lines

items: No kites or drones near lines

cards.text: Never fly drones or kites, or raise ladders and boat masts, near overhead power lines. High voltage can arc across the air gap without contact.

cards.title: The 230 V myth
cards.text: "Only 230 V" is enough to kill. What matters is the current through the body, and at 230 V a wet hand-to-hand path can easily pass more than the 30–50 mA that can disturb the heart.

quiz.q: What should you do first if someone is stuck to a live appliance?
options: Switch off the power or separate them with something dry and non-conductive
quiz.explain: Never touch them while they're energised.

quiz.q: Why are loose connections dangerous?
options: Higher resistance makes them heat up and can start fires
They lower the voltage to zero
quiz.explain: Heat and oxidation make them worse.

quiz.q: Which job should be left to a qualified electrician?
options: Adding a new circuit to the fuse board
quiz.explain: Fixed installation work needs a professional.

lessons.title: Home batteries and backup
lessons.summary: Storing solar power and keeping the lights on.

cards.title: Why a home battery?
cards.text: A battery stores midday solar surplus for the evening, raising self-consumption, and can shift cheap night energy to expensive hours. Some systems also provide backup during outages.

cards.title: Sizing a battery
cards.text: Size the battery to your evening and night consumption, not your whole day. Many homes use 5–10 kWh between sunset and sunrise.

cards.title: Hybrid inverters
cards.text: A hybrid inverter connects panels, battery, house and grid, deciding where power flows: to the house first, then the battery, then export.

cards.title: Backup is not automatic
cards.text: Many grid-tied solar systems shut down during a blackout for safety, so line workers aren't hurt by power fed back. Backup needs an inverter with an islanding switch and a backup circuit.

cards.title: Essential loads
cards.text: Rather than backing up the whole house, many systems feed an "essential loads" panel: fridge, lights, router, boiler controls, a few sockets.

cards.title: UPS for electronics

steps: UPS battery takes over in milliseconds

cards.text: An uninterruptible power supply keeps a computer, NAS or network running for minutes during a cut and allows a clean shutdown. It's rated in VA and in runtime at a given load.

cards.title: Generators

items.r: changeover switch installed by an electrician
run it outdoors, away from windows

cards.text: Portable petrol generators provide backup but must never run indoors (carbon monoxide). Connecting one to the house requires a proper changeover switch so it can't feed the grid.

cards.title: Vehicle-to-home
cards.text: Some EVs can power a home through bidirectional charging (V2H) or supply appliances via a socket (V2L). An EV battery of 70 kWh could run a typical home for days.

cards.title: Economics

items: Big price gap between peak and off-peak

cards.text: Home batteries don't always pay for themselves on savings alone. The case improves with large evening consumption, time-of-use tariffs, low feed-in prices, or a strong need for backup.

cards.title: Safety and placement
cards.text: Install batteries in a ventilated, cool, dry place, away from bedrooms and exits, with clearances as the manufacturer specifies. LFP chemistry is preferred for homes because it's more thermally stable.

quiz.q: Why do many solar systems switch off during a blackout?
options: To avoid feeding power into lines that workers believe are dead
quiz.explain: Anti-islanding protects line workers.

quiz.q: How should you size a home battery?
options: Around your evening and night consumption
quiz.explain: Store what you'd otherwise buy after sunset.

quiz.q: Where must a petrol generator run?
quiz.explain: Carbon monoxide is deadly.

lessons.title: A history of electricity
lessons.summary: From amber to the smart grid.

cards.title: Amber and the word "electric"
cards.text: Ancient Greeks noticed that rubbed amber attracted feathers. The Greek word for amber, "elektron", gave us "electricity", a term coined by William Gilbert around 1600.

cards.title: Volta's battery, 1800
cards.text: Alessandro Volta stacked discs of zinc and copper separated by brine-soaked cloth: the first battery to give a steady current. The volt is named after him.

cards.title: Faraday's discoveries
cards.text: In 1831 Michael Faraday showed that moving magnets induce currents, the basis of every generator and transformer. He had little formal education and became one of the greatest experimenters ever.

cards.title: Maxwell's equations
cards.text: In the 1860s James Clerk Maxwell wrote four equations unifying electricity, magnetism and light. They predicted radio waves, which Hertz demonstrated in 1887.

cards.title: Light bulbs

events.l: homes widely electrified in the US

cards.text: Many inventors worked on electric light. In 1879 Edison and, in Britain, Swan produced practical long-lasting carbon-filament bulbs. Edison also built the power stations and network to sell electricity.

cards.title: Electricity in Portugal
cards.text: The first electric lights in Portugal were switched on in Cascais in 1878. Large hydroelectric dams from the 1950s onward, on rivers such as the Zêzere and the Douro, powered the country's electrification.

cards.title: The transistor, 1947
cards.text: At Bell Labs, Bardeen, Brattain and Shockley built the first transistor. It replaced bulky vacuum tubes and made modern electronics, computers and phones possible.

cards.title: Nuclear and renewables
cards.text: The first nuclear power plants appeared in the 1950s. From the 2000s, wind and then solar grew rapidly as costs fell; solar module prices dropped by around 90% in the 2010s.

cards.title: Units named after people
cards.text: Many units honour scientists: volt (Volta), ampere (Ampère), ohm (Ohm), watt (Watt), hertz (Hertz), coulomb (Coulomb), tesla (Tesla).

cards.title: What's next
cards.text: Electricity is taking over more of energy use: cars, heating, industry. The challenges now are storage, grid expansion, and matching variable renewable supply with demand.

quiz.q: The volt is named after…
quiz.explain: Volta built the first battery in 1800.

quiz.q: Who discovered electromagnetic induction in 1831?
quiz.explain: Faraday showed moving magnets induce current.

quiz.q: What did the 1947 transistor replace?
quiz.explain: Transistors made electronics small and reliable.
